p:
Thank you, Chair, and hello to the MTA team. Thank you for the testimony today. I'm going to start with adding on to the questions for the express buses. Does the MTA plan to make the extend— the expanded pilot program

permanent for the QM15, 16, and 17 express bus lines on the Rockaway Peninsula?
Somebody help me here because I don't– I don't know. I don't have an answer off—
[interposing] That sounds like a yes, Chair. I'll take it.
What's the answer? Okay. Well, Lucille tells me that we are taking a look at it and we're going to come back to you timely.
Okay. Hopefully I'll be favorable. Can the MTA share data on MWBE and local hiring rates for the Rockaway Line resiliency and rehab rehabilitation project?

I can share it. I don't have it at my fingertips, but the big— that we are— we continue to be by far the largest agency on MWBE investment, over $1 billion a year, and we're thrilled about that. And that specific project, which you were very present for, which has been so successful in getting that connection to the Rockaways rebuilt on time and on budget, I don't have

the numbers offhand, but we complied with our own rules on that, and I'll give you the specifics.

And it would be great if we can follow up on that, because I'm still very much engaged on that project, and I know that initially the local numbers were not reflective of the local community, so I thank the MTA team of, you know, restarting that so that we could get the appropriate zip codes included. So I just want to make sure that we continue to monitor that progress. How does the MTA plan to allocate the $1 billion in projected annual revenues from the casino proposals? Is there— is any of this funding intended to target transportation needs in transit desert communities, such as via express bus expansions or subway or rail, excuse me, extensions?

So, the story is the governor, as part of her solution to the MTA budget challenges in 2023, allocated those casino license fees to us. And they are an absolute cornerstone of our budget and of our operating budget so that we can keep operating more service and hopefully better service. Go ahead, Jay, CFO Jay Patel.

Thank you. So as many of you know, we were– we received three license fees earlier this year. We received one in December and two in January. That $1.5 billion was programmed in our financial plan over three years. That continues to be the plan. And the first casino tax fees, right, will come to the MTA sometime later this year from the first casino that will open live later, I think, I believe in May or June. But the other two projected casinos will not open and be up and running until sometime in 2030 or '31. So the MTA would not receive any of those tax fees until that plan. But again, we have budgeted a small increment of tax fees from the casinos in our financial plan already to balance.

But at a time when there's, you know, there's a lot of challenging news that everybody sees, I mean, how good is it that thanks to what the governor and the legislature did in '23? Unlike the rest of the country, we're not cutting— you know, in Chicago and, and Philadelphia, they're talking about cutting service by 40 percent and raising fares by 20 percent. We ain't doing that. We have a secure financial situation— challenges, but

secure. And we're getting— and, and that's because of what happened at Albany.
So where's the money going to?
It goes to service. It goes to provide the A train and all, you know, the service that you—
[interposing] Look at you trying to speak my love language, the A train.

It’s going to make sure that we don't– like, unlike the rest of these big cities that are struggling with bad news from Washington on transit, that we don't have to cut and we don't have to dramatically—

[interposing] I'm sorry, Chair. I just don't want you to filibuster me, because I have about two more questions for you. So the Rockaway Beach branch, in the MTA's 20-year needs assessment for 25 to 44, MTA estimated the reactivation of the Rockaway Beach Branch would serve 39,200 riders, a 17 percent decrease when compared to the MTA's 2019 ridership estimate of 47,000 daily riders. One, what did the MTA attribute that decrease

to? And two, has there been any discussion of putting the Rockaway Beach Line into future capital plans, why or why not?

Well, I think you, you're aware of this, that we studied all the projects in that comparative valuation that led up to our capital plan. We studied all of the big new expansion projects, including the Rockaway Beach Line, and compared them for how much transit benefit and time savings they would deliver, and equity benefit, and many other things. And the one that came up really big winner was the IBX, and there are others which were okay, but they didn't at this point justify mega investment. We'll continue to study them as we go forward.
Thank you, Chair.
Mr. Chairman, next we have Council Member Hanif.

Hello and thank you, Chair. So first I'd just like to start off with what used to be in my district, 4th Avenue 9th Street Station, FGR lines. It's now in Council Member Alexa's, but we've been wanting to know about what's

happening with the lighting, the vacant stores. We've been asking both MTA and DOT and have been met with, well, it's DOT's responsibility, well, it's MTA's responsibility. It'd be really wonderful to have lighting, adequate lighting. And there have been proposals to fill the vacant window shops with art at least, but would like an update on that. And if you could share the operational cost of running paratransit. And then I'll go into some elevator and accessibility questions.
Yeah, I'm glad you mentioned elevators because, you know, your district has got three major elevator projects.
And we're really proud of that.

And one that's actually being built right now, and we've recently completed the ADA station at 7th Avenue in Park Slope. I— we, did a system-wide redo on the lighting, which we're very pleased with, and it's one of the reasons we get that much higher safety rate.
Chair, because I don't have a lot of time, could you just specifically talk about 4th Avenue, 9th Street?
I'll get back to you.
Okay, that's fine.
You don’t want to hear about what we're doing broadly on lighting?
Not, with the–
[interposing] We’ll get back to you on the specifics.

less than four minutes that I have. Okay, so $7.1 billion in new accessibility work, 60 subway stations at least will receive these upgrades. How are those stations selected and what criteria were used to prioritize them?

Okay, so the– It is done by analyzing both where the– you know, trying to make sure we have the— the goal is to have no people be no more than one station away from an accessible station. That's where we are right now. That's the pri— that's been the principal criterion. We also consult with the disability community. There has been a process, and we put it out for public comment as well, and then we make the decision. So it's been very transparent about how we're making those

decisions. And, you see the results. You've— your district has gotten three or four of them.

No, we're really grateful. And I know that the 7th Avenue FD station elevator was a real labor of love from the community for years. And, we're really, really lucky to have that elevator, especially because it's in a hospital corridor, high traffic, foot traffic area. So the MTA states that these upgrades, the $7.1 billion, will bring the system to roughly 50 percent fully accessible stations. What's the timeline for reaching that milestone, and how are you all measuring progress each year?

The end of this capital program is when we're going to be at 272 out of the 490 stations, and so we'll be at 55 percent. We've done 50 projects since 2020. We're proceeding four times as fast as the past MTAs did.
That's great news. And then how much of the accessibility investment is specifically allocated to elevators versus other improvements such as ramps, platform modifications, or ADA pathway upgrades?

I mean, technically, the elevators are not usually the biggest piece of any of those projects because what consumes a huge cost of these old stations, you got to move all the utilities around, move the stairways in many cases, move the communication system. There's a ton of work to create the space for an elevator to come in and for the mechanicals that support an elevator. But we also do all the other stuff, whether it's the platform edge, other ADA improvements as well. I'd have to get— you'd have to talk about a specific project if you want me to break it down by how much is elevators and how much is something else.
Sure. And then what steps is MTA taking to reduce elevator outages and repair times?

Well, I'm very proud of the fact we have 97 percent elevator availability, which is way, way, way higher than it used to be. To the extent that we have— any underperforming elevator in terms of availability, how frequently they break down, they tend to be these private elevators, the privately operated elevators where the city made a real estate deal, usually more than 10 years ago, and

they got a very weak agreement with a developer to put in and maintain an elevator, and those are not maintained as well. They have higher breakdown rates, but we are banging on those guys. They're not, you know, probably 10 to 20 of those elevators, but they drag the numbers down. The city— the MTA-operated elevators are actually performing in terms of availability at a very high level.
And would you be able to share what percentage of elevators and escalators—
It's in every month's report.
Every month's report, not a daily report.
The committee reports that are available online along with billions of other lines of data in the MTA Open Data system.
Excellent. And what's the average time that it's taking MTA to repair an elevator once it goes out of service? And I'll come back for round two.

Yeah, I think we've dramatically, dramatically reduced the turnaround

times for building elevators, but also for maintaining them. I'll have to– I'll have to come back to you about—
[interposing] It varies, it depends on the elevator and the situation you're dealing with, but it is reduced. We'll get you those— we'll get you those times.

Thank you. Mr. Chairman, I'd like to bring it back now to the Second Avenue Subway. In October 2025, the federal government announced a pause on funding for the Second Avenue Subway project to review contracts related to diversity, equity, and inclusion. In February 2026, the MTA sent a letter to the United States Department of Transportation in regard to $58.7 million for the phase two project of the Second Avenue Subway, which would extend the Q line into East Harlem. The Biden administration previously committed $3.4 billion to the Second Avenue Subway project as part of the Capital Investment Grant Program, which is close to half of the entire $7 billion project. Hot off the press, there is a lawsuit. Can you speak to that? And will this— the—

with the lack of the funding that we have now affect project timelines?

Okay. So, I said in my initial testimony this morning, we sued the federal government, because the Trump administration continues to withhold the Second Avenue subway funding, which they're contractually obligated to deliver. They've— for now it's been something like eight months. I think it started back in August of last year, or October [inaudible] October of this year. But there's never been any question that we were– we were in no way violating any terms of the agreement. The grant agreement between the federal government and us obligates them to reimburse us for– when we– when we put the paper in and make requisitions, and they've refused to do it. And then when we kept putting the paper in through the portal, the online portal, they shut down the online portal. So, we're just going in the– what they call the Federal Court of Claims, because it's an action on a contract to get them to release the money and let it keep going. As to your question of whether the project's gonna be delayed, so far it hasn't. But at some point we're on the verge of awarding a, you

know, roughly billion-dollar contract for excavation on Second Avenue, and we need to know that the federal money is available, and that's why we've had to take this action.
Have any con— are there any contracts? Have any contracts been awarded, and how many are left to be awarded?

Well, we've awarded— we've now awarded two major— I mean, they're small contracts, but the major contracts are the utility relocations. This is a— it's something we learned from the very imperfect first phase of Second Avenue subway is you got to move the utilities out of the way so you— they're not going to get in the way of your construction when you open up the street. So we did that as the first contract. The second contract is the tunnel boring contract, and now we are— we need— we have another major excavation contract which is close to being awarded, but we need to have resolution from the feds.
And there's no expected timeline on when the federal court of claims will resolve– resolve the dispute?
Well, they acted promptly on the Gateway dispute. So we're very hopeful that they will step in and take action.

It is my hope that they act just as promptly. In the governor's Executive Budget— Executive State Budget this year, she proposed extending the Q line west along 125th Street to my district, which of course we're all very excited for, with three new stops at Lenox Avenue, St. Nicholas Avenue, and culminating at Broadway. The governor said she will support the next phase of this project with funding for design and preliminary engineering to advance tunneling across 125th Street. Will MTA have to amend their 2025-2029 capital plan to account for this proposed extension of the Second Avenue subway?

No. So what the governor's now funded— were proposed to fund in her budget is for us to do the engineering and the other technical work that will allow us to figure out how to keep the tunnel boring machine going when it reaches what was supposed to be the terminus at Park Avenue, but around– no, Lenox Avenue, but it's around that Lexington Avenue complex, 125th and Lex complex.

We'd like to keep it going, as you said, to your district all the way to Broadway and 125th Street. We're doing the analysis that would say, how would you do that? How much time would it save? How much money would it save? But then there will have to be– once that work is done, a decision about whether we'll invest the big money to do that additional construction. I'm sure you'll be part of that conversation when it happens.
Thank you. What is the updated timeline for the project with the additional extension?

I don't— I can't tell you that offhand. It's one of the things we're going to study. How much time could we save if we kept the tunnel boring machine going? And what would that mean to the completion date of a hypothetical extension all the way to Broadway? That's one of the issues that we will answer through this year-long engineering and analysis.

I just want to go back to the World Cup, your favorite topic. The summer— this summer, the New York City region will play a host to a round of group matches and the final

match of the World Cup. U.S. Secretary— U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy today announced on March 3rd that the FTA is investing $100.3 million into public transit systems within host cities preparing to welcome millions of fans during the 2026 FIFA World Cup. Is MTA receiving any of this money?

So they had— they set up formula, which is based on how many games you had and some other variables. The New York region got $10 million of that, and we're sharing it with New Jersey. We're figuring it out. Listen, our– you know, the– our goal is for everybody to be able to enjoy the city. I'm as concerned about the fan events in Queens and the Bronx and around the city as I am about, you know, people getting to the games, which will be on New Jersey Transit. So my focus is going to be make sure that we have good service, you know, as people are moving around the city at the time of the World Cup. And we a— John has been involved in it. We're— we have a very close collaboration with City DOT talking about that planning right now.
Have you, have you received the money yet from the feds?
Not too my–
No, it hasn't been broken up yet between the agencies. But–
[interposing] And when it arrives, if— I know there's no use for free bus service for folks– for the World Cup, is your position, right? What will the MTA—
I haven't been asked to comment on it.
Fair. What will the MTA use the resources for once you do get it from the feds, assuming you do get it?

These dollars are mostly associated with security related expenses that will be associated with the World Cup. So this is, you know, policing around Penn Station where there's going to be, you know, a– you know, a very special situation as far as getting people onto New Jersey Transit through the station. So that– so that's the primary focus of this.
So fair to say for policing at the moment and security.
Mostly for security related.
Okay. But does. I have to say, I do appreciate the platform barriers being installed. I think you guys call them bolsters, is that right?
The platform barriers–
[interposing] Platform edge [sic] barriers.
Platform barriers are fine. What are— how many have been installed? I mean, how many other stations are you looking to cover? And what are the impediments to installing them at every station?

So, Governor’s given us money to— we're going to get to 200 stations by the end of this current year. I'm very proud of that. And it has— we've done, you know, we do hundreds of thousands of people in customer surveys, and that has improved the sense of safety for many people, especially older people and people with kids in the station. So we're going to have 200 stations by the end of this year, and we hope we'll find the money to keep going after that. And we're doing it with in-house labor.
I was going to ask–
Our own workforce. It's something we're also proud of. We're saving money by doing it in-house.
That was one of my questions, is whether or not you're manufacturing it in-house. What is the cost for each of these barriers?
I just can't remember off the top of my head. We did the analysis because we wanted to know whether we were going to contract it or either do in-house. And–
[interposing] You could follow up with us on that.
Yeah, yeah.

Regarding just broadly speaking, MTA and vacant lots for affordable housing, broadly speaking, New York City is obviously in the midst of an extremely difficult housing crisis. Are there any vacant lots, yards, or large-scale property the MTA has identified as defunct or no longer of use to the MTA that could be used by the city to build affordable housing?

So we were asked by the governor to come up with plans for every possible

site for housing. And I'll— why don't we just, rather than just taking time, share that with you? Because we identified all sites. As I said, though, we're— we look for opportunities. We worked something out at the end of the last administration on Atlantic Avenue where we took an MTA operating site where we, you know, we moved off of it. We split the— there was an upzoning. We took half of the site, we gave half to the city, and we got some clarification on our real estate rights on some bus facilities, one of which is in your district. So we're always working to free up space. And in the suburbs, we are taking parking lots all over the place. And with the governor's help doing housing development on them. We agree with you. Every time that— everywhere there's an opportunity for housing development, we're going to jump on it. We have a transit-oriented development group that does that every day, all day.

Well, that is certainly refreshing to hear. And our office would really like to partner with your office on, you know, potential development sites, not only in our district, of course, but throughout our city. And we also have the same, you know, same questions for DOT.

There's a DOT-owned lot along 158th Street and Riverside in my district where at any given moment you have like seven DOT cars in this massive, massive space where housing could be built. And so we really appreciate your determination to looking into these projects. I'm now going to turn it over to Council Member Wong for round two, followed by Council Member Brooks-Powers.

Thank you, Chair. My first question has to do with the express buses in my district. Ever since that– the redesign– last year, the local elected officials sent a letter to MTA regarding these bus route redesigns, specifically lack of buses or the diminishing of the frequency of buses during peak hours, specifically the QM25 and QM34 on Elliott Avenue. I use Elliott Avenue and I have seen personally that people often have to wait 30 minutes or more for the next bus, because the first one is packed. It's either wait on the cold or to get on the bus and stand. And they pay so much for the express bus, they expect to have a seat there. So my question for you is what's being done about that? Because this was raised several times already with

the DOT and with recent meetups on the MTA regarding these bus redesigns.
I think there's a dialogue that's, you know, between our offices that's moved along as– rather than me jumping in, let’s get– let's continue the discussion.
Okay.

Because we have, in some cases, seen that there is additional service warranted. And we're ready to work with you to add additional service. I'm not certain about whether it's the 34 or whether it's another line, but let's keep the discussion going because we're ready to talk about how much service there is and are there people being left on the curb.

Okay, thank you. Very quickly, second question: congestion pricing. My district pays a high proportion of the tax, and we don't see investments in our area of Queens. Can you tell me one investment being made in my district?

Well, I'll tell you what's being done in your district. We've got three accessible– ADA accessibility projects– the 63rd Street Drive, Rigo Park Station. There's new ADA at

Forest Avenue that's being paid for out of the capital program. We're– we've done the accessibility project at Woodhaven Boulevard, which is going to be finished this year if it hasn't– it's actually in the second quarter, so it's coming up pretty soon. I hope you'll join me for that celebration. We're doing huge communications and customer service upgrades at Forest Avenue and at Fresh Pond Road. We're making a lot of investments in your district, and I'm happy to get into it, you know, specifics with you. It's all– it's all above board and it's all discernible. You know, we have an MTA capital program dashboard. So I urge everybody, go online, look at your district or your area, and you can actually tap on specific projects and find out the status and learn more about them. But we'll work with you, obviously.
Okay. Thank you. And my final message to MTA. My district has expressed strongly they don't want an IBX stop. Please make a note about that.
I'm duly noted.
Thank you.
But no– I'm not responding. I'm just duly noted.
Thank you.
Okay.
Council Member Pierina Sanchez for questions.

Thank you. Thank you so much, Majority Leader, Chair, and good morning. I ran over from a different hearing. I'm very excited to have the opportunity to speak with you all today and hear your testimony. I have to say, you know, every time I see the Interborough Express mentioned, I get really sad, because it was supposed to be the tri-borough. I was at RPA, the New York director during the fourth plan process, and we really tried to get the Bronx in the picture. So, you know, I will not stop advocating for that.

You mean to say— but we got Metro North Penn Access, which is the Bronx piece of this, right? Metro North Penn Access is on the same right-of-way that that original idea called for, and we're delivering connectivity to folks in the East Bronx.

Okay, but I'm in the West, so– reach us in the South, and then I'll be happy. But my question— so I actually want to

piggyback off of Council Member Wong regarding the Bronx local bus network redesign. Chair, I just have– my concern, my complaint, and your staff is probably sick of hearing me and my team complain about this, that, you know, I understand that the redesign, you know, is delivering improvements and improving balancing of buses, but there seems to have been no consideration, or not as much consideration, of the beautiful topography that we have in the West Bronx. We have really high hills. We have really– you know, our street network is not a grid, you know, because we have these cliffs. Literally under Cliff Avenue is cut off of Bronx– the BX18 bus service that we've complained about a lot. And Assemblymember Days at the state level has also been talking about this issue. And then we have in my, you know, in the core of my area, the BX40 and 41 bus stops are not next to the train stations. Some of the stations– some of the stops that were removed were right near the transit stops. So I'm just raising that here. It feels like my concerns and our concerns have fallen on deaf ears. We just get stonewalled whenever we bring up these concerns. And it's an accessibility issue. Our seniors our folks who are on wheelchairs, they can't

get to these buses. And then there is part of the community that just feels cut off by the way that the redesign was done. So that's a comment. And then my question really is on a separate track, you know, and it's regarding, you know, understanding that the health of the MTA budget is important, and I understand that fare evasion has been an issue, but it feels like in my neck of the woods, in the South Bronx, in the West Bronx, it just feels like military. There are so many safety agents. So I just want to understand, you know, whatever you can share, whether it's the past two, three, five fiscal years, whatever you have, do you have estimates on how much revenue the MTA had been losing to fare evasion by year? And then when did the security program begin and how much has the MTA been spending on it? Are you seeing a return on investment? Or what return on investment are you seeing?

Listen, you know, the value of what we're doing is trying— as I said before, and I don't blame the riders, but there was— there's confusion. There was confusion coming out of COVID because we had a period of time when people saying get on the back of the bus, don't get on the

front, don't pay. And people got accustomed to that. And we're just trying to, like, reestablish that everybody's in this together. We are very proud of the affordability of the system, but it's not going to be there if all of a sudden everybody says it's optional. So there is, you know, you call it fare evasion enforcement, militarization. I don't see anything like that. I am in your district a fair amount. I have been there with the Eagle teams who actually get on buses and ask people to, you know, show them their proof of payment. In some cases— what? Unarmed. They're unarmed. They're not militarized in any way. And, but the important thing is that I think that we're going to soon have a system which is more like what you have in Europe, where unarmed, non-military people just get on and say, show me your OmniCard or your credit card, however you paid, so I can validate that you paid. And let's reestablish the fare payment policies of the past. I'm very proud of the fact that we did complete the Bronx bus redesign first, but it has imperfections. So let's keep talking about it, and see if we can make it better. Matching it up to the,

the subway system obviously makes sense. If there are shortcomings, keep— let's keep discussing.

Thank you, Chair. And, and I— yes, thank God they are unarmed. But I'll just share that my father was approached by someone. He had paid his fare. They, you know, whatever the conversation was, he was so nervous about it. His— and he has high— he has hypertension. He's a senior. He lives in public housing in the South Bronx. And these interactions, right, it's not— it's not— they have a uniform, they look official, they look scary, and that's the point. And we want people to pay, and I support that, but there's a balance in the communities like ours that are overpoliced, that have generational trauma around law enforcement with this heavy use. And it's not just the buses, you know, I understand that. It's also the subway stations where you have, like, three, four, five people at every single point of entry, and you have the cops, and you have— so it's just, you know, I love riding the MTA. I do agree with your testimony. I do feel safe, and I do appreciate the improvements that we've been seeing. But I just want to bring that into the conversation. The low-income people that I represent,

that I— where— that I come from, you know, that my parents are, you know, there is an impact on the stress levels and, and the mental health, their mental health of having all of this surrounding, so.
And, you know, happens— I have a woman on my right, Shanif Rieara, who actually takes the train to your district every day, Metro North and the subway.

Yeah, so we also just want to, you know, make a note that while the unarmed Eagle team agents are out there every day doing fare enforcement, we have, you know, taken a multi-step approach to remind and encourage customers that a fare is required. Every single bus, before you board, there is a message, a fare is required.
In English.

In English, but also onboard buses, I mean, and even throughout the subway network. I mean, we have, you know, published tons of customer-facing campaigns, you know, even pulling from the heartstrings. It Takes a City, and understanding that everyone has to do their part to be part of this fabric of our

neighborhoods and our community. And then also, you know, the Chairman has said fare evasion should not be a crime of poverty. So we do all— I mean, the MTA have stepped up and have been doing tons of outreach and engagement, encouraging and getting people enrolled in Fair Fares. We do it in our subway systems as well as our bus stops and high-traffic areas. So these are many steps and many approaches that we are trying to work with our riders to get them to pay their fares.
Thank you. Chair, if I may, just I would love–
[interposing] I'll allow it because you haven't had a second round of questioning. So can we just put an extra five minutes for her, please? And then—

Oh, I won't take five, but thank you, thank you so much, Chair. I just want to make sure to follow up on the numbers. I'd love to just see what is being spent. And then the last is an advocacy piece. I, you know, was a huge advocate of the Penn Access Project, but I also just want to, on the record here, state we would love to have Metro North service in the West Bronx too on the

way down. Right? Like, I would love to be able to jump on in, you know, Morris Heights and come down to the city in the morning, but our stations are skipped in the West Bronx.
Yeah, but we do have a Morris Heights station, right?
We have a station, but the train doesn't stop.

Well, we've actually increased service. I'd like to show you how we dramatically increase service. And, you know, the fastest growing piece of our mass transit system region-wide is Metro North service going north from the Bronx to Westchester and Connecticut. And people are seeking jobs and education and opportunity that way. And we love providing that service to New York City people who used to get skipped a lot more. I think we've done a lot to actually increase service to Bronxites with— on the Metro North system, and we cut the fare in half. So, something I'm proud of and committed to. Let's keep— we should discuss what– how you're looking at that service.
Excellent. Thank you. Thank you so much, Chair, and thank you, Majority Leader.

Of course. Mr. Chairman, so we're going to have an extension line coming from the east side to the west side, which is exciting. Another— to make West Harlem even more of a center of the universe, I would love— a lot of folks in the neighborhood in my district would love to see a Metro North stop along 125th Street. Can you look into that?

Yeah. So not only can we look into it, we did look into it, because it was part of the— what I mentioned before, this comparative evaluation of all of the ideas out there about major projects and extensions and expansions and so on. So when we studied the idea of having the Hudson Line of Metro North, which now comes down to Spuyten Duyvel and then zips to the east to come over the, the Harlem lift— the Harlem River Bridge, have it come straight down like the West Side. We actually studied that as an investment, and it came up as a good investment, a medium to good investment, but only if you did have 125th Street station down in

your district as well. So it's an expensive project, but one that rated reasonably highly on the rating system. You know, again, future capital programs might in fact– they'll have to be, you know, worked on but it might warrant investment in a future capital program.
Is there any way to add it to the 2025, 2029 capital program?
No. John, go ahead.

Yeah. One of the things that we're doing is we're looking at the work that's needed to be done west of Penn Station, the track configuration, so that you can run a train up the west side that goes into Penn Station from that line.
Right now there's very limited capacity to get in and out of Penn Station from the so-called Empire Line that runs up the west side. That's a technical issue that we're actually, as we say, studying.
Would you have any idea how expensive it would be to do— install a stop on 125th Street?

Real money, but not– why don't we go back and look at what's in the

comparative evaluation because there were very conceptual numbers thrown at it for the purposes of that analysis. That would be the answer to my question— your question.

It's a big transportation priority. I know that a lot of folks have, you know, have long wanted this. I understand the limitations that your agency is facing at the moment, the authority. But we can just keep conversations on that. That would be great.

Yeah. You’ll have to bring Columbia to the table, because they would be the biggest beneficiaries of all. Columbia University was— struggled to get in touch with their, you know, their conscience to pay– with your— with— as a result of your work, we're close to being able to announce that Columbia is going to pay for accessibility at the 125th and Broadway station. And they would need to be part of a solution for a Metro-North stop there, big time.

Well, of course, we hope that an agreement is reached eventually on that, and I'm sure you have more to report on that when the time is right. Regarding subway surfing— subway

surfing is the act of riding on top or outside of a moving train. In recent years, this dangerous trend has increased, potentially due to the rise in social media posts involving subway surfing. In 2023, at least five people were killed in subway surfing incidents, as compared to five total fatalities between 2018 and 2022. According to the police department, as of— the NYPD. As of October 15, 2024, the NYPD had arrested 163 people for subway surfing in 2024 year-to-date, a 22 percent increase from the 138 that were arrested in all of 2023. The NYPD contends that the increase in arrests is due to the increase in enforcement and not indicative of an increased number of subway surfers. However, in 2025, five people died as a result of subway surfing. What infrastructure enhancements does DOT— sorry, does the MTA plan on building in order to prevent youth from subway surfing?

Okay, so let's just start off by acknowledging that subway surfing is a tragedy and it is not– this is not fun. This is not hijinks. This is life or death. And we cannot have— we're going to try to— we have been working to try to discourage this. You have probably seen we have

announcements constantly in the system to educate kids. We've initiated an animated advertising campaign. We have leaned on all the social media companies to suppress this, to use their algorithms, which they're pretty good at using to get business or to find new sources of revenue. But they seem to be— not all of the, but some of them seem to be unable to suppress subway surfing videos. That one area they can't get the algorithm right. One company, Meta, principally Instagram, has been not cooperative on this. And I've called them out a couple of times. I have reached out to people through the very effective NYC Tech Group to say, we are going to have to do something about you if you don't– if you don't get with the program because you can't have kids looking at these things and getting killed. So we've been very aggressive about that. We did all kinds of things. We teamed up with New York City Public Schools students to do announcement campaigns, and so on and so on. You're aware of all that. In addition, I bless the NYPD, whatever you think of drones, to— the way they are using drones to identify subway surfers on some of these outdoor lines, which are where it principally happens, has been effective. And

I really appreciate what they've done. They have deployed officers, and it's true that there have been more arrests, but the arrests are not— no one's being incarcerated. Basically, these kids get taken off the train and they get taken home. And we ask the parents, could you please— we beg the parents, could you please intervene? Whether it's a parent or a teacher or a caregiver or coach, folks need to take responsibility for preventing kids. So there's a lot of stuff that we have done and we're going to continue doing. One thing on top of all this is it took a while, but we have developed a– and by the way, subway surfing was down in '25 versus '24. So I'm by no means declaring victory, but the number of cases actually has gone down by about 10 percent. Not— this is by no means cause for celebration, but we are pushing in the right direction. We are also on one of the lines that seems to be the worst in this area, which is the number seven. We are actually doing what we call bolsters. They're physical interventions. It's really hard to come up with a way to do this that doesn't prevent the car from being maintained in normal course. But the folks at Transit have tested out and piloted a bolster, and they're

now deploying it onto the number seven trains so that that line in particular will hopefully have– kids climbing up from between cars will be prevented to a greater extent. What else, Shanifah, am I missing?

So as part of the bolster expansion, are most of the seven train— seven train stations are going to be covered, the ones that are above ground especially? It's not the stations, it's really the physical train itself that prevents kids from climbing up—
[interposing] Got it.

between cars. And they had to test out a lot of different techniques, because again, you have to maintain access to the top of the car for maintenance purposes. But they do have a strategy that they are moving forward with aggressively, and you'll start to see more and more of those.

And my last question on this topic is, has the MTA reviewed case studies from other municipalities with metro systems to study how subway surfing is successfully prevented? If so, what ideas have been implemented?

I mean, I would have to say we are the case study. You know, we– I talked to lots of counterparts and colleagues across various transit agencies. I mean, and this is, you know, a phenomenon that is wide sweeping. But they are looking to us, and we, you know, as the chairman said, who spoke about the measures that we're taking, another thing that we're doing is going— I mean, we have the partnership with DOE students who have lent their voices to this campaign and the audio announcements, but also when we are invited in to assemblies or gatherings, we do go out and, you know, participate in doing a lot of anti-subway surfing campaigns, as well as bringing on celebrities and prominent New Yorkers to lend their voice to the cause as well.
